subject: Assumption of independence in track counts

messages.author: 47eea53ca3369f85
messages.subject: Assumption of independence in track counts
parts:
Hello everyone,

My name is Rachael and I am a relatively new user of the unmarked package. I have been using the pcount function to estimate snowshoe hare abundance across habitat types over multiple winter seasons. My data are in the form of track counts; specifically, I have 1.5 km transects that were divided into 30m segments and I counted all tracks that crossed the transect line every 30m, within 48 hours of a snowfall. Snowshoe hare are nocturnal so these counts should reflect tracks from the previous 1-2 nights. These transects were conducted multiple (3-5) times per winter over four winter seasons. I plan to analyze each year separately to satisfy the assumption of a closed population.

I am unsure whether I am violating model assumptions, and if so, how severe these violations might be in terms of interpreting my model. I am currently coding every 30m segment as a "survey", and including the transect number (i.e. each 1.5 km transect) as a site covariate. However, there is likely some spatial autocorrelation between my surveys since hares almost certainly move >30m in a given night. I was wondering if anyone else has dealt with spatial autocorrelation in track count surveys, and whether surveys need to be reasonably independent for accurate model fit. Any suggestions would be very much appreciated!

Rachael

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] Assumption of independence in track counts
parts:
Dear Rachel,

quite a standard sample design, but quite hard to properly analyse and interpret, I would say. Here are a couple of comments:

First of all, the Nmix model of Royle 2004 is probably not appropriate for your data, since it requires that each individual is only counted once. You count tracks, and I presume that it is quite possible that the same hare crosses the line multiple times within a 30m segment, thus violating this basic assumption, producing some sort of a false positive error. If you think that the problem of such multi-counting is quite common, then you *might* experiment with the Poisson-Poisson N-mixture model (see Stanley and Royle 2005, Guillera Arroita et al. 2011; also Section 6.13.2 in the AHM1 book), which does allow an individual to appear in a count multiple times. However, my own experience with this model is rather negative: it yielded what were deemed to be unrealistic estimates and I concluded that it is probably very sensitive to subtle violations of the parametric assumptions. Though of course in other situations it might perform OK.

If however you are quite confident that a hare can only be counted once per 30-m segment or perhaps if you actually follow their tracks and make sure that you only count once the hare with a track that crosses the line multiple times, then you should be fine in principle with the basic Nmix model.

If you can't exclude multiple counts and don't want to use the Poisson/Poisson Nmix model, then one of your usual fall-back positions would be some sort of Poisson GLMM, where you merely model intensity of use, which is the combination of abundance and detection rate that the Nmix models attempt to separate out. In GLMMs, it would be simple to account for non-independence of counts for 30-m segments within the same transect, either with or without spatial autocorrelation.

You could also account for spatial autocorrelation inside of an Nmix model; see Aing et al., JAPPL, 2011 (which is for an occupancy model, but for linear data along transects, and you could do the same thing also inside of an Nmix model). See Chapter 9 in our upcoming AHM2 book (very soon now !)

The other usual fall-back position for counts that are not "nmixable" are occupancy models, where you simply model presence or absence along a spatial unit. Especially if the abundance per unit is small, you may hardly lose anything by going from the modeling of abundance to that of presence/absence. About 10 years ago a couple of models were developed to account for spatial autocorrelation along trails, see these:

Guillera-Arroita, G., Morgan, B.J.T., Ridout, M.S. and Linkie, M. (2011). Species occupancy modelling for detection data collected along a transect. Journal of Agricultural, Biological and Environmental Statistics, 3, 301-317
Hines, J.E., Nichols, J.D., Royle, J.A., MacKenzie, D.I., Gopalaswamy, A.M., Samba Kumar, N., Karanth, K.U., 2010. Tigers on trails: occupancy modeling for cluster sampling. Ecol. Appl. 20, 1456-1466.

Hines, J.E., Nichols, J.D., Collazo, J.A. 2014. Multiseason occupancy models for correlated replicate surveys. Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 583–591.


About software: You will have to go down the Bayesian road for almost all of this except for GLMMs, where glmer will do, and for the trail models of Hines et al, which are implemented in PRESENCE (not sure about MARK, but wouldn't be surprised if it had them too).

That's about what comes to my mind right now.

Best regards  -- Marc

Hi Marc,

Thank you very much for the thorough response. I have been thinking (and reading) about this issue and it looks like I will be able to get my hands on some hare movement data from the same period, which I hope to use to get an estimate of how often a hare might cross a transect. I was wondering if you might have any resources for how I might incorporate these data into an N-mixture, or Poisson/Poisson N-mixture model, or other model types to estimate abundance and detection probability across my study site. I am relatively proficient at using R to apply others' code, but not so much at building my own, so any guidance on resources with code samples would be much appreciated.

All the best, and thank you again for your help!

Rachael
